name: Straight razor
lead: A straight razor, also called a cut-throat or open razor, is a single-bladed razor whose blade folds into a protective handle, known as the scales, and which is used for traditional wet shaving.[1][2] Blades are made of high-carbon or stainless steel and are sharpened by the owner or a professional by honing and stropping.[1]

Demand fell through the 20th century as safety razors and then electric razors spread, but has grown again since about 2008, with commentators citing nostalgia, long-term cost, reduced waste and craftsmanship.[1] No clinical study of straight-razor shaving for appearance outcomes was found.
infobox: Metal razors in ancient Egypt; Sheffield production from about 1680

paras: Blades are classified by point shape (round, French, square, spike, Spanish or barber's notch), by grind from flat wedge to full or extra hollow, and by width.[1] Scales are made of acrylic, celluloid, bone, horn or wood.[1] Carbon steel is easier to hone but rusts if neglected, while stainless steel resists rust but is harder to hone.[1] Grokipedia notes that a shallow blade angle of about 30 degrees is typically used.[2]

Bronze razors appear in Egypt during the New Kingdom, and gold and copper razors have been found in tombs from the fourth millennium BC.[1] Sheffield manufacturers listed narrow-bladed folding steel razors in 1680, and Benjamin Huntsman's cast-steel process around 1740 enabled hollow-ground blades.[1] A guarded razor was designed by Jean-Jacques Perret in 1762.[2]

Gillette's disposable-blade safety razor arrived in the late 19th and early 20th century, and electric razors further reduced the straight razor's share from the 1950s.[1] Interest returned from about 2008; the 2012 film Skyfall is credited with boosting sales, and the German maker Dovo reportedly went from fewer than 8,000 units a year in 2006 to about 3,000 a month.[1]

Inexperienced users may nick or pinch the skin, and round or muted points are recommended for beginners, according to Wikipedia.[1] Very thin extra-hollow blades are fragile, and Spanish points can bite during shaving or stropping.[1] Celluloid scales can combust spontaneously at high temperature.[1]

card.summary: The traditional folding open razor; popular again as a ritual and a craft, but no studies test its effect on skin or appearance.
card.note: Requires stropping and honing; cuts are a recognised risk for beginners.

quick.overview:
A straight razor is a single steel blade that folds into a handle. It was the standard shaving tool before safety and electric razors and has seen renewed interest since around 2008.

It is a grooming tool whose effects last until hair regrows. No clinical studies compare it with other razors.
quick.mechanism: A very sharp edge, kept aligned by stropping and sharpened by honing, slices hair at the skin surface when drawn at a shallow angle.
quick.risks: Nicks and cuts are the main hazards, especially for beginners. Carbon steel blades rust without care, and some blade styles are fragile or bite.
